The Power of the People

The whole history of ordinary people against the people who ruled them, from the first farming towns to today.

By Josh Pilcher
Scroll

Göbekli Tepe

Built by nobody’s subjects.

Around eleven and a half thousand years ago, people who farmed nothing and herded nothing raised circles of carved stone pillars, some more than five meters tall, and feasted beneath them. No king anyone has found told them to.

Photograph by Spica-Vega Photo Arts (Banu Nazikcan), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. The pillar enclosures of Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Türkiye, raised about 9500 BCE by hunter-gatherers. Coordination at scale, with no palace, no royal tomb, and no king anyone has found.

Verdict

Power did move from the few to the many, but only once, recently, and in one domain clearly. What rulers gained with the first states was real: the ability to tax, record, and coerce thousands who could not easily leave. What ordinary people gained after 1800 was also real, and it was specific: formal political status, meaning the vote, legal equality, and national sovereignty for billions of people who had held none of them. The qualifications are plain: that move is not demonstrated for wealth, where the richest tenth of humanity owns about three quarters of everything, not for organization, where unions have thinned for seventy years, and not in enforcement, where a right on paper could be nullified in practice for a century. When rulers appeared to lose power, the loss was sometimes a transfer, sometimes a loan recalled within weeks, and very often a change of costume, from a lord you could petition or flee to a system you cannot argue with, and any account that merges them into one rising line is selling something.

Chapter One

The World That Policed Its Bosses

For most of human history the many held one real power: they could ridicule, desert, and kill a man who tried to rule them. It worked only while four material conditions held.

Around eleven and a half thousand years ago, in what is now southeastern Türkiye, people who farmed nothing and herded nothing raised circles of carved stone pillars, some of them more than five meters tall and weighing several tons, and feasted on wild gazelle and aurochs in quantities large enough to leave mountains of bone.

The site is Göbekli Tepe, dated to about 9500 BCE. The food remains from its monumental levels are wild. There were no domesticated crops, no herds, no pottery, no writing, and no king anyone has found. Whoever organized the quarrying, the carving, the hauling, and the feeding of the workforce did it without any of the machinery later ages would treat as the price of coordination.

What the stones prove is narrow and large at the same time. Coordination at scale did not require kingship. What they do not prove is who held power instead. Ritual specialists, feast givers owed favors by everyone they fed, and coalitions of kin all fit the same evidence. The honest sentence is that a large building program ran here with no detected palace, royal tomb, or monumental temple of the kind later states built, and that the political form behind it is unknown.

The better documented world behind that scene is the world of small foraging bands, and its politics were not an absence of politics. In the bands ethnographers lived with in the last two centuries, among peoples such as the Hadza of Tanzania and the Ju/’hoansi of the Kalahari, equality was enforced, daily, by the group against anyone who reached for more.

The tools were graduated. A hunter who boasted about his kill had the meat ritually insulted, cut down to a scrawny thing not worth the walk, so that success could not be converted into standing. Generosity was not a virtue so much as a tax: demand sharing made refusal to share shameful, which made accumulation nearly impossible. A would-be leader who pushed further met disobedience, then desertion, then ostracism, and in the extreme cases recorded across these societies, the group killed him. Anthropologist Christopher Boehm named the arrangement a reverse dominance hierarchy: the many dominating the would-be dominator, together, on purpose.

It worked because of four material conditions, and the conditions matter more than the sentiment. The group numbered in the tens, so everyone could watch everyone. Nobody could store and defend a surplus worth seizing. Weapons and knowledge of where food was were spread evenly. And exit cost almost nothing. A leader whose followers walked away led nobody, and walking away was always available. This was collective coercion over individuals, including coercion of the eccentric and the accused, and in the documented cases it was largely equality among adult men in camp politics, coexisting with inequality between men and women, with feuding, and in some groups with high rates of killing. It was not a gentle order. It was an armed one that pointed its weapons inward, at ambition.

It was also not universal, and treating it as the human default is an error the record itself corrects. Where foragers could store food and defend a concentrated resource, they built hierarchy without any help from farming. On the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America, peoples who lived by salmon runs at river chokepoints developed hereditary rank, ranked houses, and institutional slavery. The difference was not character. It was that a salmon run can be owned in a way a scattered hunt cannot. Storage and defensible resources, not agriculture as such, were the hinge.

A second caution belongs in the text rather than a footnote. The foragers ethnographers described were modern people, living on the marginal land farmers and states had not wanted, after centuries of contact with both. Projecting their politics directly onto people of fifty thousand years ago is inference by analogy, not observation. Archaeology cannot recover a joke told at a boaster’s expense. What can be said is that where the four conditions held in recent centuries, the levelling machinery ran, and that nothing in the record shows it running where the conditions failed.

Early farming towns show the same lesson from the other side. At Çatalhöyük in central Anatolia, several thousand people lived for more than a thousand years in a dense town of mudbrick houses entered through the roof. Excavation has found no palace, no temple quarter, no elite district. Houses are broadly similar, and men and women appear to have eaten similar diets and done similar work. Households did accumulate standing across generations, in burials and ritual objects kept in particular houses, so inequality existed in a currency of ancestors rather than goods, and the town’s dead include a striking number of healed head wounds. The defensible claim is the negative one, and it is enough: a large, long-lived farming settlement ran for centuries with no visible stratification of the Mesopotamian or Egyptian kind. Scale did not mechanically produce a king. Who governed Çatalhöyük, and how, the record does not say.

The Indus cities of roughly 2600 to 1900 BCE make the same point at larger scale. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had planned grids, standardized bricks, drains, and standard weights used across an enormous area, and after a century of excavation they have produced no elaborate royal tomb, no palace, and no monument glorifying an individual ruler. Historian Adam Green concluded from this that a ruling class is not a prerequisite for social complexity, and his reading is a serious one. It is also disputed: the Indus script remains undeciphered, so the civilization cannot testify about itself; standardisation on that scale implies some authority that set standards and secured compliance; and other specialists read stratification and elites in the same houses and goods. The reportable fact is anomalously low visible stratification for the cities’ size. Anything stronger, in either direction, is a guess wearing the evidence as a costume. The standard ladder story, bands to tribes to chiefdoms to states, is disputed on cases like these.

So the deep past gives the story its baseline, and the baseline is often misread. Ordinary people in small groups held a real power: the power to refuse, to ridicule, to desert, and in the last resort to kill a man who tried to rule them. It was not a share of government, because there was no government to share. It governed nothing larger than a camp. And it rested on conditions, cheap exit above all, that the next development in the story set out to destroy.

Chapter Two

The Grain Machine

Writing began as accounting, and the grain state made refusal expensive for five thousand years. Athens and Rome show the two halves of the exception: depth inside a fence, and a veto that hardened into offices.

Picture the first bureaucrat. He is not a priest composing hymns and not a scribe recording a king’s victories. He is a man with a stylus pressing wedges into wet clay to record barley, beer, sheep, and the rations owed to workers, and to note which official is answerable for each. The earliest writing we have, from Uruk in Mesopotamia around 3400 to 3200 BCE, is accounting. Before the state could tell stories about itself, it learned to count what it had taken.

That order of events is the chapter in one image. Between roughly 3400 and 3100 BCE in Mesopotamia and Egypt, a new stack of capacities came together, and each piece reinforced the others. There was a staple crop that could be taxed: grain ripens at a predictable time, grows visibly above ground, divides cleanly, stores well, and travels, which makes it assessable and confiscatable in a way that root crops dug piecemeal from the ground are not. There was writing, which gave the state a memory longer than any subject’s and made a debt or a labor obligation enforceable years later. There were walls, specialised soldiers, and officials whose only job was the machinery itself. And there was an ideology that placed the king between his subjects and the gods, holding the calendar and the rituals as well as the granary.

Historian James C. Scott made the grain mechanism famous, and in the riverine grain states of Mesopotamia it is strong: the earliest states are grain states, and the fit between the crop and the tax collector is too exact to be coincidence. As a universal law it is weaker. States elsewhere extracted labor service and mixed staples through other counting systems, and reviewers have shown that early polities drew on a spectrum of foods and fiscal devices rather than grain alone. The mechanism that generalises is not wheat. It is any surplus an administration can see, count, and store, including labor itself.

What the stack changed, concretely, was the arithmetic of refusal. A forager upstart faced a camp that could leave by morning. A subject of an early state faced an organization that held his name on a ration list, knew his harvest, could call on soldiers who did nothing else, and could pass all of that to a son. Extraction became repeatable and hereditary, which is precisely what no band dominator had ever achieved. The costs of the new order are written in skeletons: in many early farming and state populations, stature fell, teeth rotted, and women’s bones record years of grinding grain. Though those costs track crowding and diet as much as kingship, since a stateless farming town shows them too.

Egypt shows the pole of the system, a kingship that claimed divinity and endured, with interruptions, for three thousand years. It also shows the limits inside the pole. Provincial governors and wealthy priesthoods held ground the center could not always retake, and around 1152 BCE the royal tomb builders of Deir el-Medina, unpaid in grain, downed tools and marched on the temples in what is often called the first recorded strike. They were not citizens and they won no rights. They withheld the one thing the state needed from them, at the one moment it could not be replaced, and they were paid.

That is the pattern of popular power inside the early states, and it held for millennia. Flight was the structural check. State reach was shallow, transport was foot and river, and beyond the taxed core lay land that was empty or hard to govern. Desertion was chronic enough to shape policy, and early wars were often fought for captives as much as for territory, because people were the scarce resource and people kept leaving. Inside the walls, the everyday repertoire ran from foot dragging and false compliance to pilfering and arson, the unglamorous resistance that official archives, written by the state, systematically under record. Open revolt existed from the beginning of the record. None of it governed anything. All of it set a price on governing, and rulers who ignored the price found their tax base walking into the hills.

Assemblies complicate the picture, and they are older and wider than the famous Greek case. Councils of elders and armed men appear in Mesopotamian texts, consulted on war and judgment, though the evidence is largely epic and legal material rather than minutes, and the founding scholar of the idea, Thorkild Jacobsen, conceded that the record cannot cleanly separate a primitive democracy from a primitive oligarchy. In India, the gana sangha polities of the first millennium BCE rejected monarchy and decided by council, drawing their members from particular lineages. In central Mexico, Tlaxcallan governed itself without a king into the sixteenth century, through a council that Spanish accounts put at about a hundred members. Every one of these bodies excluded most of the people who lived under it.

Athens remains the outlier, and its numbers state both halves of the truth. In its democratic centuries the assembly of citizens decided war, law, and exile, juries and the council of five hundred were filled by lot, and pay for service let poor citizens actually attend. The citizens numbered perhaps 30,000 to 60,000, roughly 10 to 20 percent of the population. Women, the enslaved, and foreign residents, together the large majority of the people in Athens, held no share at all. Participation inside the citizen body was broader and deeper than anything before the modern period. The citizen body itself was a fence.

Rome produced the ancient world’s most instructive mechanism. In the long Conflict of the Orders, the plebeians, the commoner class excluded from high office, repeatedly withdrew from the city in organized secessions. The founding walkout of 494 BCE comes to us through Livy, writing centuries later, so the story is tradition; the institutions it explains are solid fact. The plebeians won tribunes, officers who were legally untouchable and could veto official acts, written law in the Twelve Tables, access to offices, and by the Lex Hortensia of 287 BCE the rule that plebeian resolutions bound everyone. Note what made it work. The plebeians were organized, they were needed as soldiers, and their refusal was collective and repeatable. They did not persuade the patricians. They made themselves a body the state had to bargain with, and the bargain hardened into offices that outlived any single crisis. The system still weighted votes toward wealth, the Senate still ran foreign and financial policy, and women, slaves, and most Italians stood outside it. It ended not in popular rule but in civil war and an emperor who absorbed the tribunes’ powers into his own person, which is a lesson about where veto offices can be parked.

Two questions organize everything in this era, and they must be asked separately because they have different answers. Did a concession create a body that outlived the crisis and the ruler’s recovery, and did that body hold resources of its own, money, arms, organization, or a way out? And separately: how many people did it actually cover? Rome’s tribunate passes the first pair and fails the second. The Deir el-Medina strike fails the first and was never meant to pass the second. A check on a ruler is not the same thing as power in the hands of the ruled, and the ancient world is full of the first and nearly empty of the second.

The era’s verdict is a movement in the opposite direction from the one the report’s title suggests. Power moved from the many to the few, slowly, unevenly, and for about five thousand years incompletely, because most human beings still lived outside states, between them, or at their shallow edges, where flight stayed cheap. What the many invented under the pressure were the counter mechanisms every later era would reuse: the strike, the secession, the council, and the walk into the hills.

Chapter Three

The Bargain Centuries

Concessions extracted at sword point lasted eighteen days. What lasted was paper rulers could sell, towns that could pay, and parliaments built by creditors, none of it held by the peasant majority.

On 14 June 1381, on a field at Mile End outside London’s walls, a fourteen-year-old king faced a rebel army that had entered his capital the day before and killed his chancellor and his treasurer in the Tower. The rebels’ demands were concrete: abolish serfdom, end the poll tax, remove the ministers they called traitors, and let land rent at fair rates. Richard II granted charters on the spot. The next day, at Smithfield, the rebel leader Wat Tyler was cut down by the mayor of London in the king’s presence. By 2 July, eighteen days after Mile End, the charters were revoked. At least 1,500 people were killed in the suppression that followed.

Everything about the bargain centuries is in those eighteen days. A concession extracted at sword point, by people with no institution to hold it, lasted exactly as long as the emergency that produced it. What the revolt did change was a price. The flat rate poll tax, imposed three times in four years and hated because it charged the poor at the same headline rate as the rich, was abandoned by England as a fiscal form after 1381. The revolt had raised that instrument’s political price beyond what it yielded. That is a veto, not a transfer, and the distinction runs through the whole period.

The centuries after Rome’s fall in the west are usually introduced as the weakening of kings, which they were, and then misread as the strengthening of the people, which they mostly were not. When central power fragmented among armed landholders, the bargaining space that opened was filled by lords, bishops, towns, and guilds: organized bodies with walls, money, and lawyers. The peasant majority, in much of Europe bound to the land as serfs owing labor, fines, and obedience to manorial courts, did the work and funded the bargains other people struck.

Magna Carta is the period’s most famous document and its most misread. On 15 June 1215 King John, who had squeezed his barons with repeated heavy levies to fund failed wars in France and then lost London to them, sealed a charter of sixty three clauses at Runnymede. Most of it is a feudal grievance list: inheritance payments, wardships, widows, fish weirs. Two clauses outlived their century. Clause 39 said no free man could be seized, imprisoned, or dispossessed except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land. Clause 40 promised that right and justice would not be sold, denied, or delayed to anyone. The enforcement clause, clause 61, empowered twenty five barons to seize the king’s castles if he broke the deal.

As an act of the people it fails at the first line. The free man of clause 39 excluded the unfree majority of the population, who gained nothing and in places were secured more firmly for their own lords. As a settlement it failed within weeks: Pope Innocent III annulled it on 24 August 1215, and civil war resumed. What survived was not the charter’s enforcement machinery, which was stripped out at the first reissue, but the paper. A minority government reissued revised versions in 1216 and 1217 to buy baronial loyalty during a civil war, and the definitive 1225 reissue was an explicit sale: the kingdom’s great men granted the king a fifteenth of their movable goods, about 40,000 pounds, and the charter was the receipt. Edward I confirmed it onto the statute roll in 1297. The people’s part of Magna Carta is real but it came centuries later, when seventeenth century lawyers such as Edward Coke reinvented a baronial tax bargain as a universal charter of rights, and the myth became a resource that much wider groups could spend. The durability was manufactured, by reissue politics first and myth making second. Both facts belong in the story, and neither makes 1215 a popular victory.

Towns were the period’s genuine machine for converting money into freedom. From the eleventh and twelfth centuries, sworn associations of townspeople across Italy, Flanders, the Rhineland, and northern France bought, negotiated, or fought for charters granting personal freedom, market rights, their own courts, and fixed taxes. The bargain had a face. A serf who reached a chartered town and lived there for a year and a day unclaimed was free: the German legal maxim said town air makes you free. He worked, he kept to the town, the year ran out, and the lord who had owned his labor had lost the claim. It was a real rule, with real exceptions, and it worked because towns had what peasants lacked, concentrated wealth a ruler needed and walls he had to reckon with. Guilds had the same double face: self government inside, monopoly against outsiders.

Parliaments grew from the same soil, and the soil is the finding. David Stasavage’s finding is that assemblies with real powers over tax consent were stronger in compact city states than in large territorial states, and that merchant-dominated assemblies secured cheaper credit for their governments. In part, representation was a device by which creditors monitored a king they were lending to. Parliaments, councils widened to include non nobles, emerged in Europe only where rulers had first fostered self-governing towns. War created the need. The communes created the counterparty. Where there was no organized body of taxpayers, there was nothing for a hard-pressed king to bargain with, and no parliament grew.

Iceland shows the limiting case and the strangest failure mode. From 930 the Icelandic Commonwealth ran a national assembly, the Althing, with lawmaking and courts and no king, no army, and no executive at all. Thirty nine chieftains, the godar, sat in the law council, and free farmers chose which chieftain to follow and could transfer their allegiance to another, a working exit option inside the system. It lasted until 1262. It was not overthrown by a tyrant or defeated by the people. Chieftaincies concentrated in a few families, the island slid into civil war, and Icelanders submitted to the Norwegian crown. The check oligarchised from within. Power was lost sideways, to concentration among the supposedly empowered, with no ruler’s reversal to blame, a failure mode the standard story has no box for and the modern world has several.

The Black Death ran the period’s cleanest experiment, and its result is a warning against reading demography as destiny. The plague of 1347 to 1351 killed somewhere between three tenths and six tenths of Europe’s people. In England, labor scarcity did what revolt could not: despite an Ordinance in 1349 and the Statute of Laborers in 1351 trying to freeze wages at pre plague levels, real wages rose by roughly half by the 1390s, and mid fifteenth century English real wages reached levels not seen again until about 1880. In much of Eastern Europe the same scarcity produced the opposite: lords who controlled courts and markets more completely answered scarce labor by binding it tighter, and the second serfdom that followed lasted into the nineteenth century. Scarcity is leverage only where institutions and exit options let workers spend it. Where lords held the courts and the roads, scarcity was a reason to lock the door.

The revolts themselves follow a bleak arithmetic. The French Jacquerie of 1358 was crushed within weeks. The German Peasants’ War of 1524 to 1525, the largest popular rising in Europe before 1789, put forward in its Twelve Articles demands that communities elect their pastors, that serfdom be abolished, and that common woods and waters be restored, and was destroyed by professional armies in the spring of 1525, with deaths estimated at 70,000 to 100,000. Pre modern rebels were effective as warnings: taxes were not reimposed, dues were not raised, hated officials were sacrificed. They were ineffective as governments, because they lacked administration, siegecraft, pay, and a program for running a territory. Victory, when it came at all, required a split above them. The one clear peasant win of the era proves the rule by its mechanism: in Catalonia, after decades of remensa peasant struggle, the Sentence of Guadalupe in 1486 abolished the abusive customs of serfdom for a payment, delivered by a king who needed peasants as a counterweight against his own nobles. The peasants’ freedom was real, durable, and a by product of a fight above their heads.

Outside Europe, rulers were constrained too, and the constraints teach the same separation of variables. In the Ottoman Empire the sultan was formally bound by sacred law, and its interpreters, the ulema, could issue a legal opinion, a fetva, that legitimized a sultan’s deposition. It happened repeatedly, from Osman II in 1622, who was killed, to Abdülhamid II in 1909. Janissaries, the empire’s standing infantry, acted as a capital city veto group until a sultan destroyed them in 1826, and provincial notables bargained with the center as a matter of routine. Scored on constraint, this is a strong result: an institution that survived centuries, held by men with independent wealth and arms. Scored on who held power, it is zero for the population. The checks protected corporate order and law. No assembly consented to taxes, and no subject gained a protected share of rule. When provincial notables tried to formalize their position in a deed of agreement in 1808, the sultan signed it and then spent two decades destroying them. A charter whose counterparty does not survive is a truce.

China built the opposite device: legitimacy that was conditional in theory and unusable in practice. The Mandate of Heaven, used to justify the overthrow of the Shang dynasty around 1046 BCE and sharpened by the philosopher Mencius, held that a ruler who governed badly forfeited the right to rule, and that floods, famines, and successful rebellion were the signs. Emperors were also slowed in daily practice by a professional bureaucracy, by censors licensed to remonstrate, and by the sheer thinness of the state on the ground, with a single county magistrate governing perhaps two hundred thousand people through local gentry. But there was no body that could legally say no and survive saying it. The Mandate named no refusal body, no court, council, or electorate authorised to declare it lost. The feedback therefore arrived in the only form available: rebellion, at catastrophic scale. The Taiping rising of 1850 to 1864, led by a repeatedly failed examination candidate, held Nanjing for eleven years and killed, on published estimates that run from 20 million to 70 million, a toll no census can settle. The dynasty survived only by handing military and fiscal power to regional armies, decentralizing the empire it saved. Historians warn that the dynastic cycle, the tidy pattern of rise, decay, and fall, is partly a moral template later court historians imposed on messier change, and it should not be mistaken for a mechanism. What is usable is the structural point: two thousand years of conditional legitimacy produced dynasty replacing dynasty, and never subjects becoming citizens.

Why did some rulers’ power erode and others’ not? The cases converge on dependence. A ruler who needed his subjects’ money and soldiers every year, and faced them organized, bargained, and the bargains sometimes hardened into institutions. A ruler with revenue that bypassed his subjects did not. Spain is the control case: American silver flowed to the crown without passing through the Cortes, and the Spanish parliament’s leverage withered accordingly. France is the other: the Estates General was not summoned at all between 1614 and 1789, while the crown built extraction machinery, tax farming, the sale of offices, and royal intendants, that raised money without consent. England after 1688 shows the bargain at full strength, and its beneficiary precisely: Parliament controlled supply, the Bank of England followed in 1694, and the state’s borrowing costs fell because creditors trusted a king who could not easily default on a parliament of lenders. The ruler lost the right to tax at will and gained a larger, cheaper revenue in exchange. Both sides could win the bargain, which is why it lasted, and the people, in any franchise sense, got nothing from it for another 144 years.

Technology cut both ways for the same reason. Gunpowder artillery favored whoever could afford siege trains and new fortifications, and it dissolved castle based noble independence. Cheap infantry weapons and mass conscription later favored whoever could mobilize the population. Printing multiplied whatever fragmentation already existed: in Europe’s patchwork of jurisdictions a banned printer crossed a border and kept printing, while movable type in China and metal type in Korea, centuries earlier, operated inside unified empires and produced no comparable political break. A technology does not distribute power. It reprices cooperation, and the price lands on whoever was already organized to collect it.

By 1800, then, the ledger for the majority was modest and mostly indirect: labor dues commuted to money rents in the west, a century of higher wages after the plague, town freedom for those who reached a town, courts that sometimes ruled for a subject against an official. Constraint on rulers had grown in specific places, impressively. Power held by the ruled, as a protected share in governing, had not. That is the baseline the next two centuries have to be measured against, because measuring them against a golden age of charters flatters them.

Chapter Four

The Great Concession

After 1800 the vote, legal equality, and sovereignty moved to billions of people, priced by war, taxation, and threat. Wealth did not move with them, and the organizations that won the bargain have thinned for seventy years.

In the winter of 1918, men stood in uniform who could not vote, and women filled the munitions factories who could not vote either. They had been conscripted and called on, their bodies and their labor taken at a scale no earlier state had attempted, and they could not plausibly be told they were unfit to choose a government. Then the Act arrived. The Representation of the People Act gave the vote to all men over twenty one and to women over thirty who met a property condition, and the electorate roughly tripled at a stroke. The vote was part of the price.

That exchange, dependence priced in rights, is the engine of the only period in the record where power demonstrably moved from the few to the many, and the move has to be stated with its qualifications attached or it is not demonstrated at all. What moved, measurably, was formal political status. In 1800, on the standard regime codings, no country in the world was a democracy and almost everyone lived under a closed autocracy. By the late twentieth century, billions of people held electoral rights, legal equality, and the protection, however uneven, of courts. What did not move with it: wealth, where concentration today rivals the levels of the age before the concession; organizational power, which peaked mid century and has fallen since; and enforcement, which lagged the law by generations in the places that needed it most. Hold all four facts at once and the period comes into focus. Drop any one and it becomes a poster.

The British sequence shows the concession arriving in instalments, each one priced. The Reform Act of 1832, passed under real fear of revolution, still left only about one in seven adult men able to vote. The Chartists, the first mass working class movement, demanded manhood suffrage, the secret ballot, and equal districts in petitions Parliament rejected in 1839, 1842, and 1848; nearly the whole Chartist program was law within eighty years, delivered piecemeal once governing factions found uses for pieces of it. The act of 1867 roughly doubled the electorate, enfranchising urban male householders under a Conservative leader who expected many of them to vote Conservative. The act of 1884 took the figure to about 60 percent of men. Then 1918, then equal terms for women in 1928. The pattern is not a dam breaking. It is a series of transactions, in which threat, war service, partisan calculation, and organized pressure each did part of the work and none did all of it.

The American sequence carries the enforcement warning in its purest form. Property tests for white men fell state by state by 1856. The Fifteenth Amendment of 1870 barred racial exclusion from the vote in law. Across the South, poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence then nullified it in practice for about ninety-five years, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 put federal enforcement behind the paper right. The next year in Mississippi, a Black voter registered with federal protection behind the registration, the paper right finally backed by the government that had written it. Women’s suffrage arrived nationally in 1920, the voting age fell to eighteen in 1971 under the pressure of a draft that sent eighteen year olds to Vietnam, and the global firsts are startlingly recent: New Zealand in 1893 was the first self-governing country to enfranchise women, France waited until 1944, and Switzerland until 1971. Universal adult suffrage, the supposed baseline of modern politics, is younger than many living voters.

Labor organization was the concession’s second pillar, and for ordinary people it was the one that changed Tuesday rather than election day. Legal unions, the eight hour day won country by country after 1919, and collective bargaining converted an individual worker, who could be replaced by Friday, into a counterparty. The American density series measures the rise and the long fall in one line: about 35 percent of workers were union members at the peak in 1954, and 9.9 percent in 2024, with private sector density around 6 percent against about 32 percent in the public sector. The welfare states built in the same decades proved more durable than the organizations that won them, because a pension or a health service is defended by every voter who expects to use it, while a union must be rebuilt in every workplace in every generation. Entrenched entitlements do not negotiate, strike, or set wages. They are what organized power leaves behind when it weakens: real protection, in a form that cannot bargain for more.

Decolonization moved power on a scale nothing else in the century matched, and it too splits into two variables. United Nations membership rose from 51 states in 1945 to 117 in 1965, and in 1945 roughly 750 million people, near a third of humanity, lived under colonial rule. Independence transferred sovereignty, genuinely and permanently, from empires to nations. It did not automatically transfer power within those nations: many new states became one-party or military regimes within a decade of the flag raising. Both halves are the finding. A transfer between levels is not a transfer down to the population, and counting independence as popular power without the second step repeats, at global scale, the error of counting a charter as a people’s victory.

Why did rulers concede at all? The mechanisms recur across the cases, and they are mechanisms of dependence, not of enlightenment. Credible threat mattered: franchise extensions cluster after revolutionary shocks, in 1848, in 1918 and 1919, and after 1945, because elites who believed refusal might cost them everything bought stability with inclusion. War mobilization mattered most of all: mass armies and mass taxation turned the ordinary person into a counterparty the state needed every year, and the suffrage and welfare settlements of both world wars were priced accordingly. Taxation bargaining mattered where the state lived off its own citizens’ incomes and needed their compliance; where rulers lived off oil, minerals, or foreign aid instead, the bargain broke, the modern form of the Spanish silver that had freed a sixteenth century crown from its parliament. Elite splits were the proximate cause in nearly every successful transition, because mass pressure works through a crack in the ruling coalition, and a crack without mass pressure produces a palace reshuffle rather than a transfer. And organization decided what a concession was worth the morning after: the same legal right was a weapon where unions, parties, and a press existed to use it, and a decoration where they did not.

The reversal mechanisms were visible from the start, because the concession was never a ratchet. It depended on conditions, and the conditions changed. Professional volunteer armies, drones, and capital intensive warfare reduced the state’s need to bargain with a mass public for soldiers. Globalised production let employers route around organized labor. Resource rents freed governments from taxpayers. And the modern technique of reversal turned out to be cheaper than the old one: not repealing rights, but hollowing them, by packing courts, capturing media regulators, rewriting electoral rules, and prosecuting opponents, one institution at a time, with the forms intact throughout. A charter once had to be annulled by a pope or a battle won against it. A right can now be drained by administration, which lowers the price of taking power back below anything the earlier centuries knew.

The measured result, on the verified figures, is a peak and a long, uneven decline from it. The V-Dem Democracy Report of 2025, with data to the end of 2024, counts 91 autocracies against 88 democracies, the first time autocracies have outnumbered democracies in over twenty years, with 72 percent of the world’s population, 5.8 billion people, living in autocracies, and only 29 liberal democracies. Freedom House’s 2025 edition records a nineteenth consecutive year in which more countries declined than improved, 60 against 34, with about 20 percent of the world’s population living in countries rated Free. These instruments code formal institutions and liberties as experts judge them; they do not measure what a person’s day feels like, and the step from falling scores to falling lived power has to be argued, not assumed. It also has to be argued in the other direction: the decline is measured from a real peak. Formal inclusion in 2000 stood at a level no earlier century approached, and most of the legal gains of the concession era still stand somewhere, defended, in many places, by voters who punish attempts to remove them outright.

Set against the wealth figures, the period’s shape is stranger than either the celebration or the lament. The World Inequality Report of 2022 estimates that the richest 10 percent of humanity takes 52 percent of global income and owns 76 percent of global wealth, while the bottom half takes about 8.5 percent of income and owns 2 percent of wealth, and that since the mid 1990s the richest 1 percent captured 38 percent of all new wealth created while the bottom half captured 2 percent. Historian Walter Scheidel argues that across ten thousand years only mass mobilization war, transformative revolution, state collapse, and lethal pandemic have sharply compressed inequality. His evidence for the four cases is strong and his conclusion is contested: critics note that the horsemen usually worked through the legislation that followed them, and that the Nordic compressions were largely legislative achievements, built under war’s shadow but written in parliaments. What is not contested is the mid century compression itself, when top income shares in the belligerent democracies fell sharply and stayed down for a generation, legislated, taxed, and built into housing, education, and health systems. It is the strongest evidence in the whole record that a transfer can be real, broad, and durable at once, and it was made by organized majorities with parties and unions at full strength, in states that had just depended on those majorities for survival.

So the great concession was real, and it was conditional. It stalled and partly reversed when the dependence thinned and the organization decayed. Nothing about it was a law of history, and nothing about its partial reversal is either.

Chapter Five

The Ground Level Now

The collector a person could argue with became a system no one can argue with. Alone, a person of 2026 has less usable leverage than a peasant facing that collector; organized as a class, the same person holds instruments that have killed nationwide systems.

Between 2013 and 2015, the state of Michigan let a computer system decide who had committed unemployment insurance fraud. There was no human review. The system treated silence as confession: a questionnaire posted to an online account a claimant no longer used, unanswered within ten days, could become a fraud finding with penalties of up to four times the benefits received. About 40,000 people were falsely accused. When the state auditor reviewed roughly 22,000 of the determinations, 93 percent did not involve fraud. The state eventually settled the class action for 20 million dollars, and about 3,000 people were in the compensated class, a small fraction of those the system had accused, because a timeliness ruling cut the rest out.

Hold that case next to the tax collector of an earlier century and the present distribution of power comes into focus. The collector could be argued with, evaded, bribed, shamed by neighbors, or outwaited, and he could also be arbitrarily cruel. The system cannot be argued with at all. It has no mercy and no cruelty. It acts before the citizen knows anything has happened, it repeats its error identically for everyone in a class, and when it is wrong there is no person in whom the decision lives. The citizen’s task is no longer negotiation. It is correction of a record, proving a negative to an entity that does not experience doubt.

The same architecture reaches an ordinary person in 2026 through half a dozen channels at once, and most of them never involve a human official. Tax comes first, and it comes before the citizen does: for wage earners the employer withholds the tax and reports the payment, so the money is never held and refusal never quite becomes an option. The compliance figures measure the mechanism precisely. Income subject to withholding is misreported at about 1 percent. Income subject to little or no reporting is misreported at about 55 percent. The payroll record is the modern grain: visible, divisible, storable, and reported by a third party, and the 4.5 billion or so information returns flowing to the tax authority each year are its harvest. The citizen’s side of the bargain is time, an average of about twelve hours and 290 dollars per return, and roughly 6.9 billion hours a year across the United States.

Benefits run on procedure, and procedure rations what law grants. In one large American study of food assistance applications, nearly two in three new applications were denied and more than half of those denials were procedural, a missed form, a missed interview, a missed deadline, rather than a finding that the applicant was ineligible. Australia ran the automated version at national scale: a scheme that averaged annual tax income across fortnights and treated every mismatch as a debt issued hundreds of thousands of wrongful debts before a federal court ruled the method unlawful and a royal commission found it had been unlawful from the start; settlements reached 1.87 billion Australian dollars. In the Netherlands a risk scoring system linking government databases was struck down by a court in The Hague in 2020 because its model was too opaque to verify, and a related childcare benefits scandal, in which about 26,000 parents were wrongly accused of fraud, brought down the cabinet in 2021. The incentive structure is identical in each case. The agency banks the savings from automation immediately. The cost of error lands first on the claimant, in garnished wages and lost coverage, and reaches the agency only years later, if litigation or an inquiry succeeds.

Work is governed the same way, by persons replaced with systems. The foreman became a rate: warehouse software that counts a worker’s time off task and disciplines against a target no supervisor chose that morning. The hiring manager became a screening report the applicant pays to be judged by and often cannot see first. The landlord became, in part, a pricing system: the American justice department’s case against the RealPage software alleged that competing landlords, feeding their rents into one algorithm, coordinated prices without ever meeting, and the resulting proposed settlement would restrict how the software may use their data. In gig work the classification fight shows the direction of travel in both jurisdictions that decided it most visibly. In California, after courts and the legislature moved toward employee status, voters passed Proposition 22 in 2020, which restored the contractor model the platforms had written. In Britain, the Supreme Court’s Uber ruling granted drivers the narrower intermediate status of worker, not full employee rights. Print the outcomes, not the slogans: in the largest American market the platforms won the classification they wanted, and in Britain drivers won something real and smaller than employment.

Private rule setting now sits alongside state rule setting, and the two borrow each other’s strength. A handful of firms intermediate most of the world’s search, social communication, phone operating systems, cloud computing, and payment rails, and they set enforceable rules on speech, payment, and access for billions of people without elections, without due process, and with exit priced by network effects: leaving means leaving everyone else. States, for their part, increasingly govern speech by setting the penalties and duties under which those firms moderate, so a removal arrives as a private terms of service decision even when the incentive that produced it was statutory. The European Union’s Digital Services Act fines run to 6 percent of worldwide turnover, and Britain’s Online Safety Act to 10 percent, and age checks now attach identity to reading in ways anonymous print never required.

The surveillance layer underneath all of this is documented, and one famous part of it is a myth worth correcting precisely because the correction is more instructive than the myth. China’s social credit system is not a single algorithmic score grading every citizen. Read against the policy documents, by scholars including Rogier Creemers and Jeremy Daum, it is a fragmented set of blacklists and compliance records, aimed mostly at firms and at people who have defied court judgments. A person is on a list or off it. Listing carries real consequences, restrictions on air travel and luxury purchases among them, and it enforces existing judgments rather than inventing new offenses. The commercial product that fed the Western image, Alibaba’s Sesame Credit, was voluntary, separate, and denied a credit license. China’s camera networks, real name registration, and platform data collection are real and documented on their own evidence. The instructive point is the comparison: the Dutch scoring system and the Chinese blacklists are the same family of mechanism, database matching and list based exclusion, and the difference in outcome is not the database. It is that a Dutch court could order the system stopped, and did.

Identity is the gate key that makes the other channels addressable. India’s Aadhaar system counts about 1.34 billion live holders and processed more than 27 billion authentications in a single recent year, which means a fingerprint mismatch at a ration shop can stand between a person and food, with an alternative route that exists in law and is uneven in practice. In the United States, enforcement of the REAL ID standard for domestic flights began in May 2025. Where no alternative route exists, an error in the identity layer propagates into every service built on it, benefits, banking, travel, work, in the same way a wrong record in a benefits system propagates into a debt.

What can the person on the receiving end do back, and what does it cost? Start with the defendant who never appears. In debt collection, the largest single category of American civil cases, a defendant who does not come to court loses by default, and in reporting jurisdictions more than 70 percent of cases end that way. The judgment still lands, and at least one side is unrepresented in about three quarters of American civil cases, with no right to a lawyer in them. That is the chapter’s second finding: the remedies are real, and they are priced for institutions. Voting is the cheapest act and the weakest unit: it decides who governs in aggregate and can do nothing for a wrongful debt this month. Information requests run against a growing queue, and protest carries a tail of arrest and fines. Jury service remains the one unmediated power on the list, laypeople inside the state’s own process whose verdict no official can administratively revise.

The pattern across the remedies is the pattern across the channels, reversed. Individual answers almost never move a system. The Michigan fraud machine, the Australian debts, and the Dutch scoring model were not stopped by any individual’s appeal; Robodebt’s losses before tribunals were simply not published by the government that kept losing them. They were stopped by collective vehicles: class actions, funded litigators, ombudsmen whose warnings built a record, journalists working from released documents, and courts with the power to kill a rule everywhere it ran at once. The same uniformity that replicates an error across a whole class replicates a remedy to all of them when the rule falls. That symmetry is new in history, and it is the strongest card the many hold in 2026.

It has to be set against what the many have gained in daily life, because a report that counts only the state’s reach is rigging its own scales. Exit from a job, a marriage, a church, or a home town is cheaper and less punished than at any earlier point in this record. Literacy is near universal where it was a minority attainment in 1800. A private person can publish to the world at no cost, document an abuse as it happens, and organize across a country in a day, instruments no earlier population possessed. Legal rights against the state are broader and more often enforced than in any prior era, and peaceful transfers of power after bitter elections still occur, in Brazil, Poland, Senegal, and elsewhere in just the last few years. Even closed autocracies now stage elections and claim popular legitimacy, a tribute no eighteenth century monarch felt obliged to pay. The ground level verdict is therefore a split, and the split is the finding. Alone, facing withholding, a procedural denial, a default judgment, or a blacklist entry, the ordinary person of 2026 has less usable leverage than a peasant facing a collector who could at least be met. Organized, as a class, a voting bloc, a union, or a court case with a name that stands for thousands, the same person holds instruments that have killed nationwide systems with a single judgment. Power moved from persons on both sides to systems on both sides. The many win when they arrive as a system. They lose, routinely and procedurally, when they arrive one at a time, which is how the modern state almost always arranges to meet them.

Chapter Six

Two Rival Reads

Was the great concession a real transfer now in partial reversal, or a change of costume, from rulers a person could see to systems no one can argue with? Two coherent answers, and the evidence that separates them.

Read A: The transfer was real, and the present dip is a reversal inside a real story On this read, the great concession happened and can be pointed to, not inferred. Suffrage extensions were not repealed in most places once granted. Legal equality survived the regimes that granted it. The mid century compression of income was legislated and lasted a generation. Decolonization did not reverse. These are not forms. A woman voting in France in 1945, a Black voter registered in Mississippi in 1966 under federal protection, and a pensioner drawing a benefit as of right rather than as charity were exercising power their grandparents could not have exercised at any price, and calling that a costume change requires explaining away the lived difference, which this read declines to do.

The decline since roughly 2005 is, on this read, exactly what it looks like: a reversal, partial and uneven, driven by named mechanisms, executive capture of courts and media, the decay of unions and mass parties, and warfare that no longer needs mass consent. It is measured from a real peak, and the resilience evidence cuts for this read as much as against it: most countries rated Free in 2005 were still rated Free two decades later, voters have repeatedly punished would-be autocrats at the ballot box, and in South Korea in December 2024 a president’s martial law declaration was reversed within hours by a parliament that voted it down while citizens filled the streets. Systems built by the concession defended themselves, which is what a real transfer predicts and a pure costume change does not.

This read answers the strongest evidence against it directly. Wealth concentration is conceded as fact and denied as refutation: political power and wealth were never the same variable, and the concession was a transfer of the first, incomplete in the second from the start. Union decline is conceded as the reversal’s main domestic mechanism, which is why the read calls the present a reversal rather than a continuation. The lived power evidence, cheaper exit, broader rights, unprecedented speech reach, is not an embarrassment to this read. It is part of the transfer’s substance, and it is precisely what a reversal would eventually have to take away, which gives the dispute a testable edge.

What would decide it: enforcement and responsiveness data, tracked over time. If policy in the countries where scores have fallen continues to track median voter preferences, if citizens keep winning against the state in court at undiminished rates, and if the index declines fail to predict declines in lived experience over the following decade, this read weakens and the dip was shallower than the instruments claimed. If responsiveness to the median voter decays where executives consolidate, if win rates against the state fall, and if the declines in formal scores are followed, country by country, by declines in exit costs, speech reach, and benefit security, the reversal is confirmed as substantive and this read stands.

Read B: The costume changed, and the conditions that once made refusal work are gone On this read, stated at full strength, power did not move from the few to the many. It moved from persons you could see, petition, flee, or kill to systems you cannot, and every supposed transfer was captured at the moment of transfer by an intermediary class that the standard story never lists as a ruler. Writing created scribes who outlasted kings. Charters and parliaments formalized a bargain between crown and capital, with assemblies serving in part as devices for creditors to monitor the kings they lent to, while the peasant majority of the same centuries was being enserfed more tightly in the east. Suffrage was repeatedly granted as a governing technology, by Bismarck to outvote liberals inside a constitution built to contain it, by a Conservative leader in 1867 who expected the new voters to vote Conservative, and across the record whenever a ruling faction needed allies against a rival and calculated that inclusion could be priced to leave the levers untouched. Decolonization transferred sovereignty from one elite to another, and many of the new states were one-party or military regimes within a decade. The platforms completed the sequence: rule setting over speech, payment, and work for billions, exercised by firms no one elected, appealable to no one, with exit priced by the network itself.

The measurement, on this read, is the tell. Count forms and the transfer is real. Count outcomes and the same record supplies the opposite numbers: the wealth shares in Chapter 4, the union line, 35 percent to under 10, and the Fifteenth Amendment, a formal transfer long nullified in practice in the South. A gift granted because the giver calculated it cost less than refusal is a purchase of stability, priced by the seller. What was lent can be recalled by administration, and the modern literature on hollowing, courts packed, rules rewritten, media captured, forms intact, is the recall in progress. It is not the reversal of a completed transfer. It is the revelation of the terms.

Deepest of all, on this read, the one form of popular power that demonstrably worked is extinct. Forager refusal rested on cheap exit, no storable monopoly, evenly spread weapons and knowledge, and groups small enough to watch each other. Storage, enclosure, passports, and a fully partitioned planet destroyed every one of those conditions, and nothing since has restored any of them. There is no hillside left that is not also a tax registry. Ridicule, the cheapest sanction in the oldest repertoire, does not work on an institution with no face, and a citizen cannot desert a database. Impersonality is not the dilution of power. It is its armour.

This read meets the strongest evidence against it directly. The system kills in Michigan, Australia, and the Netherlands are conceded, and their terms are the point: each took years, institutional funding, and a collective vehicle, each compensated a fraction of those harmed, and the identical mechanisms expanded unchecked wherever no court held the power to stop them. A remedy that requires a royal commission is not a counterweight in daily operation. It is an occasional correction to a standing asymmetry. South Korea’s parliament reversing martial law in hours is the hardest case for this read, and it answers it on its own terms: the reversal ran through an institution, a legislature with its own resources and legitimacy, which is intermediary power checking executive power, the oldest pattern in the record, with the crowd as witness and pressure rather than as holder.

What would decide it: the intermediary audit and the agenda test. Track the size, security, and policy influence of the unelected administrative class, civil services, courts, central banks, party machines, and platform rule makers, across each supposed transfer of the last two centuries. If any major transfer measurably shrank or subordinated that class, this read is wounded at its center. If none did, and if the share of major legislation originating in mass organizations has fallen since about 1970 even as franchise breadth peaked, the costume thesis is confirmed in the two numbers that matter. Run alongside it the refusal index: the practical cost to an ordinary person of saying no, to an employer, a landlord, a benefits system, a platform, a state, measured in outcomes rather than legality. If refusal against systems has grown cheaper on net, this read falls. If refusal against persons grew cheaper while refusal against systems grew dearer, and the system share of life kept growing, it stands.

Chapter Seven

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

Whether citizen resources predict which democracies hold. Score countries now on the resources citizens independently control, union density, media ownership concentration, party membership, local government fiscal autonomy, and court independence in practice, and watch whether those scores predict which states hollow out over the next decade better than regime labels do. If they predict, the report’s lens is validated and the defense of popular power is a resource question, not a forms question. If they do not, both rival reads need rebuilding.

The automation of benefits and its court record. Automated eligibility, fraud, and debt systems are spreading through welfare states faster than the case law that governs them. Each new SyRI, Robodebt, or MiDAS, and each jurisdiction that adopts one without a judicial stop, is a live measurement of whether the collective remedy can keep pace with the system’s replication speed. A major system surviving a full legal challenge on its merits, rather than on procedure, would mark a genuine shift in the balance.

War’s changing price. The historical bargain ran on mass armies and mass taxation. Watch whether states fighting serious wars with professional forces, drones, and borrowed money can sustain them without conceding anything to their populations, and whether any state that returns to mass conscription finds itself bargaining again within a political generation. A large war fought at scale with no domestic concession would retire the oldest mechanism in this report. A conscription state forced to bargain would revive it.

Rentier revenue and the tax bargain. Every government that funds itself from resource rents, sovereign borrowing against them, or a narrow base of mobile capital is a test of the fiscal dependence mechanism. Watch the states whose oil income falls fastest: if declining rents produce taxation, and taxation produces demands for representation that gain institutional form, the mechanism is confirmed in real time. If they substitute surveillance and borrowing and concede nothing, the mechanism’s conditions have changed and the report’s medieval control case stops travelling.

Exit, priced. Watch the practical cost of leaving: emigration restrictions and exit taxes, platform portability rules that do or do not let a person take their audience, customers, and records with them, non compete enforcement, and housing costs that lock workers to places and employers. Exit was the foundation of the oldest popular power and the quiet variable under every later one. A decade in which exit gets measurably cheaper for ordinary people would be the first since the frontier closed, and it would change the analysis more than any election.
